opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I was not a particularly standout student when I was little. I grew up in China, and the school system there is very structured. There's a lot of emphasis on exams, memorization, and following the curriculum. I think I did fine, but I wasn't the kid who was top of the class in everything.

What I remember more is that I was always curious about how things worked. I liked taking things apart, playing with gadgets, and reading things outside of what was assigned. Sometimes that curiosity didn't line up perfectly with what school rewarded, because school was more about getting the right answer on the test than exploring why something works.

Looking back, I think that tension was actually useful. It taught me discipline, because you had to put in the hours. And it made me value the moments where I could just explore on my own. That combination, being able to grind through fundamentals but also wanting to tinker and build, is something I still rely on today in research.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Xu was not a standout student and describes exam-focused schooling, but does not attribute her performance to disliking classes or exams.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses structured academics, curiosity, discipline, and independent exploration, but does not describe school primarily as a social place.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I was not a standout student for most of my childhood. I grew up in China, and the school system there is very exam-driven, very structured. You're ranked against your classmates constantly, and I remember being somewhere in the middle of the pack and feeling like that was just who I was.

What I did have was a kind of restless curiosity that didn't fit the format very well. I liked taking things apart, figuring out how a toy worked, that kind of thing. I spent a lot of time on the computer, and not always for schoolwork. My parents were patient about it, maybe more than they should have been. But that tinkering turned out to matter more than my test scores did.

The shift for me came later, when I had a bit more freedom to choose what I studied. Once I could pick problems I actually cared about, I became a much better student almost overnight. I think that taught me something I still carry into how I run my lab now. A lot of students who look average on paper are just waiting for the right problem. So when I meet a student who's struggling in a class but lights up when they talk about a side project, I pay attention to that.

r001.rationale: The response says Xu was middle of the pack in an exam-driven system and had curiosity that did not fit its format, but it does not attribute her school performance to a strong dislike of classes or exams.

r002.rationale: The response discusses school as structured and exam-driven, but does not describe it as primarily a social place.

astra-6.text: I think school was a mix for me. I enjoyed learning and figuring things out, but I didn’t always enjoy the structure of being told what to learn and how to learn it. When something caught my interest, I could spend a lot of time on it. So there was sometimes a gap between what I was curious about and what I needed to do for class.

r001.rationale: The response says she sometimes disliked school’s structure, but it does not attribute poor performance to that dislike or mention classes and exams.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe school as primarily a social place.

sol-6.1.text: I don’t remember school as one single experience. There were moments when I was really curious and excited to learn, and other times when it felt more like figuring out what answer the teacher expected. Those are quite different things—understanding something for yourself and learning how to do well in school.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts curiosity with trying to give the expected answer, but does not attribute poor performance to a strong dislike of classes or exams.

r002.rationale: The response discusses learning and school expectations, not school as primarily a social place.
